subject: math
objective: Explain why the base case and inductive step together prove P(n) for every n at or above the base, explain why assuming P(k) is not circular, write a complete induction proof for a summation or inequality claim, and identify which part of a flawed induction proof fails.
sources: Levin O. Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, 3rd ed., Section 2.5: Induction (https://discrete.openmathbooks.org/)
Rosen K. Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, Chapter 5: Induction and Recursion
Golomb SW (1954). Checker boards and polyominoes. American Mathematical Monthly 61(10): 675-682 (https://doi.org/10.2307/2307321)
misconceptions: Assuming P(k) is circular, or is the same as assuming the conclusion
The base case is a formality that can be skipped
Checking many examples proves a statement for all n
The inductive step only has to work for most k, or for large k
It is fine to start from P(k+1) and derive P(k)
Inequality steps must reach the target exactly rather than any bound at least as strong
The base case must always be n = 1
modelLimitations: The domino model shows ten dominoes and asserts that the line continues; it illustrates, but does not replace, the well-ordering argument given in the text.
Uses n = 1 as the default starting point; notes that some courses start the naturals at 0.
Workshop proofs are multiple choice; students do not write free-form proofs in the browser.
Strong induction is mentioned only in the proof template summary.
The tiling activity shows boards up to 16x16.
